analysis.one_liner: Requires retailers with loyalty-card data to directly notify customers during food recalls.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a Republican with a Democratic cosponsor, never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee and received no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Department of Health and Human Services require grocery stores and other food retailers that already track customer purchases to send direct recall notices — by phone or email — to people who bought contaminated or mislabeled food. Retailers would be reimbursed for those costs by the manufacturers, importers, or distributors responsible for the contamination. Ignoring a recall order would become a prohibited act under federal food law.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers who bought recalled food but never saw a public announcement. Public recall notices often miss people who bought the product days or weeks earlier; direct notices using purchase records reach them. Consumers would also gain because contaminated food gets out of kitchens faster, reducing illness.

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary of HHS could order any food retailer to report whether it has a system capable of identifying who purchased the recalled food, and if so, to issue a recall notice to those buyers, by methods such as phone calls or email [S2][S3].

Retailers would be reimbursed for recall notice costs by the manufacturers, importers, or distributors identified as most likely responsible for the contamination, so stores would not absorb the expense of protecting shoppers [S2][S3].

Failing to comply with a recall order would become a prohibited act under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, giving the government an enforcement tool against companies that ignore recalls [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers, importers, and distributors responsible for adulterated or misbranded food would pay the cost of retailer recall notices. Retailers would face new compliance duties, though their costs would be passed back to the responsible party.

drawbacks.text: The bill only covers retailers that already have a system to identify purchasers; it expressly does not let the Secretary require stores to build such a system, so many shoppers — those buying at stores without purchase records — would get no direct notice [S3].

Retailers would take on a new legal obligation to send recall notices, and the reimbursement process — which requires HHS to identify who 'most likely caused' the contamination — could invite disputes over who ultimately pays [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: direct recall notices would reach buyers that public announcements miss, reducing foodborne illness. The costs are modest and shift to the party that caused the contamination. The main design weakness is that coverage depends entirely on which stores already track purchases, leaving a gap for shoppers at stores without such records.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee three weeks later, and sat there until the Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Castle, a Republican, introduced the bill on April 2, 2009 with Rep. Jane Harman as cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S4][S5].
On April 21, 2009 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was recorded before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food manufacturers and retailers avoided the new recall-notice obligations and reimbursement requirements, while shoppers who buy recalled products remained reliant on public announcements.

for.name: Rep. Michael N. Castle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

against.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Committee leadership never reported the bill out; after its referral to the Health Subcommittee, no markup or floor action was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican from Delaware sponsored the bill and a Democrat from California cosponsored it; there were no roll-call votes.

industries.note: Stores would face a new duty to notify customers who bought recalled food, but only if they already track purchases, and HHS would order the responsible manufacturers to reimburse their costs. Many large chains already run loyalty programs, so the marginal burden would be modest.

Firms identified as most likely responsible for contaminated or mislabeled food would have to reimburse retailers for recall notice costs, adding to the existing expense of recalls. Ignoring a recall order would become a federal prohibited act.
Retailers may satisfy the notice requirement through third parties they select, so firms that run customer-communication systems would gain new business.
